newsitem.title: USA: J.C. Penney buys Eckerd for $2.54 billion in cash/stock.
newsitem.headline: J.C. Penney buys Eckerd for $2.54 billion in cash/stock.

text.p: Consolidation of the nation's drugstore industry took another step forward Sunday as J.C. Penney, owner of the Thrift drugstore chain, said it agreed to buy Eckerd Corp. for cash and stock valued at $2.54 billion.
With the addition of $760 million in Eckerd debt, the deal is valued at $3.3 billion, the companies said.
The acquisition would be Penney's second in the rapidly consolidating drugstore industry since August, when it agreed to buy Fay's Inc. for about $285 million.

Eckerd, based in Largo, Fla., operates 1,724 drug stores in 13 states and 542 Eckerd Express Photo labs in 11 states. Its operations are concentrated in the Florida and Texas markets, and spread across the Southeast.

Plano, Texas-based Penney, in addition to its department stores, operates 450 drugstores under the Thrift or Treasury brands. It also is in the process of incorporating another 271 Fay's stores in upstate New York and Pennsylvania as well as 200 Rite Aid stores.
The addition of Eckerd will give it approximately 2,800 retail drug stores stretching across the Northeast, Midwest and the Sunbelt, with combined sales projected at $10 billion for fiscal 1997.
The deal, which is to be completed in two stages, has been approved by the boards of directors of both companies.
Penney said it will launch a $35 per share cash tender offer for about 37.1 million shares, or 50.1 percent, of Eckerd, whose stock closed at $28.75 Friday on the New York Stock Exchange.

The balance of the purchase will be made through a stock swap, in which Eckerd shareholders will receive 0.6604 of a Penney share for each Eckerd share, based on Penney's closing price of $53 on Friday, also on the NYSE.
Penney said its board of directors approved plans to buy back 15 million shares to complete the share exchange, which calls for the company to issue about 24 million shares.

The Thrift/Eckerd deal follows last week's agreement by Drugstore giant Revco D.S. Inc. to buy regional chain Big B Inc. in a sweetened takeover valued at $380 million, and a deal earlier last month in which Rite Aid Corp. agreed to buy West Coast chain Thrifty PayLess Inc. for $1.4 billion.
Eckerd had been viewed as a possible bidder for Big B, which had rejected Revco's initial offer.

Rite Aid, currently the largest drugstore operator in terms of number of stores, had signed a pact to buy Revco for $1.8 billion, but that deal collapsed after regulators expressed concern that the union would raise consumer prices.
